newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan April-June GDP data. [Corrected 7:59 gmt]
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan April-June GDP data. [Corrected 7:59 gmt]

text.p: Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) fell a real 0.7 percent in April to July from the previous quarter, official data showed on Friday.
This would translate into a drop of 2.9 percent on an annualised basis, the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast on average a drop of 1.1 percent from the previous period. Analysts' comments follow:
MIKIHIRO MATSUOKA, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DAIWA INSTITUTE OF RESEARCH: "These numbers are within expectations, so there will be no change in the response of the markets."

Matsuoka expressed some concern about the recovery in the second half of the year. "I'm not sure if the second half of this year will be as strong as the EPA (Economic Planning Agency) expects. We have a very weak situation in inventory adjustment and we see consumption only modestly recovering and capital expenditure may come to a halt."
JESPER KOLL, HEAD OF RESEARCH AT J.P. MORGAN

"I think that basically all is well with the Japanese economy. Private (corrects from "public") sector demand is taking over as the engine for growth. Most important, capital expenditure has seen...six consecutive quarters of growth."
Koll added that he thought the economy would remain on track for recovery in the second half of the year.
JANE BERRYMAN, SENIOR FIXED INCOME ANALYST, TECHNICAL DATA

"Private demand taking over from public indeed is a very good sign. I still think that going forward, there are still some spotty signs in this economy because not all the sectors are moving forward all together. That's probably the green light for the BOJ to keep policy accommodative. The main thing for them (markets) is that we're going to be remaining accommodative this year and possibly well into 1997 as well. I would imagine JGBs are seeing little bit of pressure on that."

"Possibly the yen is also chopping back and forth. Ultimately though, I think we'll see the market stabilising when it realises the green light is on for the BOJ to remain accommodative. That's the message in these figures and that's all that really matters for the market.

"I think the government can read anything it likes into these figures. It can either say, ah, we're still not in full recovery mode, it still looks weak...still in recovery, may not be the right timing. Or, they can choose to be optimistic. They can say ah-ha, an improvement from the previous quarter, see that. We are coming out of recovery, our policies are wonderful. Everything is working."
HIROSHI SUZUKI, ECONOMIST, NORINCHUKIN RESEARCH INSTITUTE

"Looking at the recent data, it's within an expected range. We had forecast minus 1.5 percent quarter-on-quarter in July, so compared to that the numbers are rather strong. But this is not enough to change the government's view on the economy -- that it's still gradually recovering."
